summary: An early Telnet option, from 1974, that lets the two ends of a connection negotiate vertical tab stops for output, meaning the lines on a page where a vertical tab should land. It is a companion to the horizontal tab options by the same author. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 656 defines a Telnet option for handling vertical tab characters in output. The two ends of a connection can agree who handles them and which line positions are tab stops.

subtitle: A Telnet option for agreeing on who handles vertical tab stops and where they are.

tldr.problem: When output contains vertical tabs, the sending and receiving systems need a way to agree on who handles them and which line positions count as stops.
tldr.mechanism: The NAOVTS option lets the sender and receiver negotiate responsibility and exchange line numbers for vertical tab stops.
tldr.outcome: The unit metadata marks RFC 656 as Historic. It defines option code 14 and rules for assigning vertical-tab handling.

today: RFC 656 is Historic according to the unit metadata. It defines the NAOVTS Telnet option and has no later update or replacement listed in the unit.

sections.title: The NAOVTS Option
sections.content:
RFC 656 defines NAOVTS, or Negotiate About Vertical Tabstops, as Telnet option code 14. It concerns output on a simplex connection between a data sender and a data receiver. The option lets them negotiate which side handles vertical tab stops and what those stops are.

If the sides agree to negotiate but do not exchange further subnegotiation messages, the receiver is assumed to handle the vertical-tab behavior. The default option state is DON'T NAOVTS/WON'T NAOVTS.
sections.plainLanguage: NAOVTS is a Telnet option for vertical tab characters. It gives the sender and receiver a way to agree who handles them.

sections.title: Negotiating Responsibility and Stop Positions
sections.content:
The sender can propose handling through a value of 0. Values from 1 to 250 give line numbers, measured from the top of the page or screen, and suggest that the other side handle the stops. A value of 255 asks the other side to handle them without suggesting positions. Values from 251 to 254 are not allowed.

If neither side wants to handle vertical tabs, the receiver must do so. If both want to handle them, the sender does so, because the RFC assumes the sender may know more about the data. Either side can disable further negotiation with the appropriate DON'T or WON'T command.
sections.plainLanguage: The sides can exchange line numbers or say which side should handle vertical tabs. If both want to handle them, the sender takes responsibility; if neither does, the receiver must.

sections.title: Subnegotiation Messages
sections.content:
After option negotiation, either party can send a subnegotiation message with values that describe responsibility and stop positions. The data sender uses the DS command, whose code is 1. The data receiver uses the DR command, whose code is 0. More than one stop value is allowed only when each value is greater than 0 and less than 251.

The RFC says a party should not propose a state that is already in effect, except to refuse negotiation. Changes should be acknowledged, and a refused option should not be proposed again until something changes, such as a new process starting.
sections.plainLanguage: Once they agree to use the option, the sender and receiver can send subnegotiation messages with stop positions. They should acknowledge changes and wait for a change in circumstances before repeating a refused proposal.
